state.misconception_label: Believes f(x - a) translates the function up a units

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: What transformation maps the graph of \(y=f(x) \) to the graph of \( y=f(x-3) \). I got Translation by vector
\(
\left[\begin{array}{l}
0 \\
3
\end{array}\right]
\) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's clarify the misconception here. When we have \( f(x-a) \), it actually translates the function to the right by \( a \) units, not up. So in this case, the graph of \( y=f(x-3) \) would be a translation to the right by 3 units, not up. Can you explain how this understanding changes your initial interpretation of the transformation?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so it's to the right, not up! So the translation vector would be like... [3, 0] instead? But I'm still a bit confused about why it's to the right when it says minus 3 - wouldn't minus mean it goes left?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's clarify this further. Remember, when we have \( f(x-a) \), it actually shifts the graph to the right by \( a \) units. So in this case, when we have \( y = f(x-3) \), it means the graph shifts to the right by 3 units. The negative sign in front of the 3 indicates a rightward shift, not a leftward one. Can you see how this adjustment changes your understanding of the translation now?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher correctly identifies and addresses the specific misconception about vertical vs. horizontal translation, but repeatedly tells rather than elicits reasoning, and the student's final turn shows they still don't understand why minus 3 causes rightward movement, indicating the misconception persists.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher repeatedly states the rule without providing worked examples or clear explanations of why f(x-3) shifts right, instead just asserting the fact multiple times, which fails to demonstrate the comprehensive explanatory approach characteristic of traditional teaching.
